She has three honest answers available and one dishonest one. The dishonest one is saying yes at nine in the evening and finding out on Thursday what it cost her.

## First decide whether it is even a change

A clarification makes an agreed piece clearer. A change adds work, replaces work, or makes you redo work that was finished.

The test is your plan, not the tone of the message. Open your piece list and ask one question: does anything on it have to be added, made longer, or done again? If nothing moves, it is a clarification. Answer it and carry on. Asking which of two agreed layouts you meant is a clarification. Adding a size chart to forty products is not, however small each one is on its own.

Do not decide this from memory. A request that felt tiny in a chat window looks different once you are looking at the pieces it touches.

## Name what it moves before you name anything else

Open the plan and find every piece the request lands on. New pieces, longer pieces, finished pieces that now need redoing. Add up the working days. Then follow the sequence forward and find the date that moves as a result.

That last one is the fact the client actually needs. "That adds about a day" tells them nothing they can act on. "That moves the launch review from Tuesday the 14th to Thursday the 16th" gives them something to decide about.

## The three shapes an answer can take

Every change reply is one of three arrangements, and none of them is a plain yes with nothing moving.

Add it and move a date. Swap it for something already agreed, keeping the date. Park it for a second phase once this one closes.

Your job is to lay out the choice and let the client pick. How that reply is worded, so it reads as helpful rather than as a refusal, is the client communication course's subject. What the change is worth and how you charge for it belongs to the freelancing course. What belongs here is the record and the date.

## The change note

Keep one short log per client, sitting with that client's plan. Six columns: date asked, what was asked, what it moves, the options you offered, what was decided, date decided.

Append to it, never overwrite it. That log is the reason you can answer "when did we agree that" in a sentence, instead of scrolling a chat thread for twenty minutes.

Nothing starts until the decided line has a date in it. A yes in a chat thread counts. A yes on a call does not, until you have sent the one paragraph summary and they have answered it. Put the whole change in that message, the way chapter one put the whole scope in the message you wanted reacted to, and end it with a question that can only be answered yes or no.

## Where the collision actually lands

The change note lives with that client's work. The date it moves lands somewhere else, on the one list you keep across every client.

Mila's size chart adds two working days to the skincare store. Those two days sit inside the week she already promised a Cavite client their content calendar. The size chart conversation is not finished until she has looked at that week. This is the failure that gets called disorganised later, and it is not disorganisation. It is a change agreed inside one client's world by someone who forgot they live in four.

## The small favour that arrives five times

Sometimes absorbing something is the right call. It genuinely takes ten minutes, the client has been easy to work with, and the conversation would cost more than the task.

Absorb it. Then write it in the log anyway, with the decided line reading "absorbed, no date moved".

Two reasons. The fifth time the same favour arrives, you are not arguing from a feeling that you are being taken advantage of, you are reading a list back. And when the arrangement comes up for renewal, that list is the only evidence any of it happened. Goodwill nobody wrote down is goodwill nobody remembers.

A change nobody put a date against was not agreed. It was mentioned.

## Set up the log before the next message arrives

Open a document for whichever client is most likely to ask for something extra this month, and put six headers on it: date asked, what was asked, what it moves, the options offered, what was decided, date decided. Leave it empty. The next "while you're in there" message is the one that finds it waiting.

lessons.title: Saying a date will slip, early
lessons.content_mdx:
# Saying a date will slip, early

Rowena took a bookkeeping catch up for a hardware store in Cebu: eight months of unrecorded transactions, agreed at six weeks. In week four she told the client it would be late. By then there was nothing left to decide. There was an apology, and a client rearranging something on their end that they could have rearranged a month earlier.

The information that the project was in trouble already existed in week one. She just did not treat it as information.

## The signals are all boring

None of these look like an emergency. That is exactly why they get past you.

- An approval or an answer is past the date you gave it.
- Something you need from the client has not arrived, and you have quietly stopped asking for it.
- The first piece you finished took far longer than your own record of timings said it would.
- A piece has been sitting in progress for several days with nothing you could hand to anyone.
- You have stopped opening that client's board.

The last one is the most reliable and the least comfortable. Avoiding a board is a decision your hands make before you make it. When you notice you are avoiding one, that is the client to look at first.

## Week one has options. Week four has an apology.

Early, a slip is a choice between things: cut a deliverable, move a date, change the order, chase an approval harder. Late, every one of those has expired and the only thing left is the date going past.

So the reason to raise it early is not honesty as a virtue. It is that early is when the client can still do something, and a client who was handed a choice remembers the project differently from a client who was handed news.

## What the message contains

Four parts, in this order.

**What happened.** One sentence. No story, no build up.

**What it affects.** Name the deliverable and the date. Not "the timeline". A client cannot decide anything about a timeline.

**Two options.** Both real, both things you would actually do.

**What you need from them, and by when.** A decision is a task with a date, like anything else.

No apology paragraph. One line of regret if the cause was yours, then get to the options. Three paragraphs of sorry asks the client to manage your feelings on top of their own problem, and it reads as somebody who thinks the apology is the deliverable.

Two options means two. "Move the date or I work faster" is one option and a promise you should not make. Real pairs look like this: the full agreed set on a later date, or a reduced set on the agreed date. Or: the piece they need for their launch first, and the rest two weeks after.

## Rowena's message, if she had sent it in week one

Here is what week one could have looked like, with the four parts written out in full rather than described.

Subject: Hardware store catch-up, statements needed

Hi Mang Ramon,

What happened: Two of the eight months of bank statements I asked for on Oct 3 still have not arrived, and I am now at the point in the schedule where I need them to keep going.

What it affects: The catch-up is scheduled to finish Nov 14. Without the September and October statements, that date is no longer realistic.

Two options: I can hold Nov 14 if the statements arrive by this Friday, Oct 24. Or, if getting them will take longer than that, I reconcile the six months I already have now and finish the last two once the statements land, so the bulk of the work is not stuck behind the missing two.

What I need: Let me know by Wednesday, Oct 22, which of these works better for you, or send the statements directly if that is faster.

Rowena

Sent in week one, that message costs Rowena nothing and gives Mang Ramon a real decision. Sent in week four, the same four parts would have nothing left to offer, because both options would already be gone.

## When the delay is theirs

State the dependency and the date it was due, then stop. No blame sentence. The date does the work, and adding a line about how long you have been waiting turns a fact into an accusation the client now has to defend against.

Then give them the arithmetic. Delivery becomes a set number of working days after the statements arrive, so the date moves with them rather than with you. That sentence is far easier to write when the dependency was already on the plan with a date attached, which is why chapter two put it there.

## When you do not know yet how bad it is

Raise the signal anyway, with a date for the answer.

"The first section took longer than I planned for. I am re-estimating the rest today and will send you either a revised end date or confirmation that the current one holds, by Thursday."

That message costs you nothing and buys you the right to send the second one.

## After the decision

Whatever gets agreed, write it back in one short message and then re-date the board. Cut deliverables come off the piece list. Remaining pieces get their new dates. The status of everything affected changes.

A recovery agreed in a conversation and never written into the plan stops being true within about a week. Then you are running the old plan while the client is remembering a different one, and the next surprise is worse than this one.

Going quiet is the single move with no upside in it. A client who has not heard from you fills the silence with the worst version, and the worst version is always worse than whatever is actually happening.

## A question worth asking before you close this tab

Which board have you stopped opening this week? Sit with the answer for a moment rather than dismissing it. That is the client to look at today, while the options are still cheap.

lessons.title: The handover, and the work it brings back
lessons.content_mdx:
# The handover, and the work it brings back

Ending a project badly costs you more than running one badly. A client who had a rough eight weeks and a clean ending will hire you again. A client who had a smooth eight weeks and then spent a month chasing you for a file will not, and will say so when somebody asks about you.

## A handover is a transfer, not a delivery

Sending the files is the part everyone does. Four things make it an actual handover.

**Final deliverables where the client can find them.** In their storage, owned by them, named so a stranger could pick the right file. Not a link into your drive that you might reorganise next year.

**Access and ownership out of your accounts.** List every account and tool the job touched: the store, the courier account, the scheduling tool, the analytics, the shared mailbox, the domain. For each one, either the client already owned it and you had access, or you opened it and it now has to sit with them rather than with you. Move the ownership where the account allows it, take yourself off where the job is finished, and write down what you no longer hold.

Not every account can be moved. A payment or merchant account is usually registered against the business's own documents, so it cannot be signed over: the client opens theirs and you come off yours. Check what the specific account allows rather than assuming, and treat an account that cannot move as its own line in the handover.

Account security is a subject of its own and this is not it. The point here is narrower: a project is not closed while a client's business depends on your email address continuing to exist.

**A short walkthrough for anything they operate themselves.** A recorded screen walk of the thing they will actually do every week, or a page of numbered steps. Short is a requirement, not a style preference. Nobody watches forty minutes.

**Loose ends named.** Everything you know is unfinished, imperfect, or waiting on somebody else, written in a list with who holds it. A loose end you name is a professional's note. The same loose end discovered in March is a complaint.

## The close out message

The close out message confirms the job is finished against the definition of done you agreed at the start, back in chapter one. That is what it is for. It lists what was delivered against what was agreed, names the loose ends and who owns each one, states what access moved, and asks the named approver to confirm.

That confirmation is the thing that ends a project. Without it, projects do not end, they fade. A faded project is one a client can reopen six weeks later on the grounds that nobody ever said it was finished.

## Your own review, before anything else

Half an hour, alone, with the plan open. Four questions.

Which estimates were wrong, and by how much? Put the real timings into your record, so the next job you quote is built on a bigger sample than this one was.

Which piece ate the time? There is usually one, and it is usually not the one you were worried about.

What did you do that was never in the scope? Each of those is a line in the next scope's exclusions, written in the words the client used.

What did the client do that slowed things down? That is a client dependency you write differently next time, with a date attached and a note on what happens when it is late.

This half hour is where the next project gets easier. It is also the part nobody does, because the job is finished and finished feels like the reward.

## The ask, made once

The moment the client confirms the work is done is the highest point of their opinion of you, and it does not stay there. Three things, one message, right then.

**The testimonial.** Ask for a sentence about something specific. A client asked for "a few words" writes something generic that helps nobody. A client asked "would you write a line about how the weekly updates worked for you" writes something a stranger can actually use.

**The referral.** Name the shape of the business you want next. "If you know another clinic still taking bookings by hand" is answerable. "Anyone who needs a VA" is not a question, it is a shrug, and it gets a shrug back.

**The next piece of work.** Either the thing you noticed while you were inside their business, or a standing arrangement to keep running what you just built.

Ask once, then stop. A second ask two weeks later reads as pressure and costs you the referral you had already earned. Put the client on a list with the date instead, and go back when you have something specific to say to them. Building that list out into your next clients is Freelancing Fundamentals' job.

What this course claims is smaller. The project you close cleanly is the one still available to come back to.

## Before you file this client away

Pull up the last project you finished. Check it against the four handover items and the ask: files in the client's own storage, access moved or noted as unmovable, a walkthrough recorded, loose ends named, and the ask sent once. Whichever item is missing is the one to fix this week, while the client still remembers the job fondly.

quiz.prompt: Joel is writing website content for an inn in Baguio. The agreed scope is English copy for twenty room pages. In week three the owner messages: "Small tweak lang, can we have the room descriptions in Tagalog too?" What is Joel's first move?

options.text: Reply that it is a small addition he is glad to help with, then fit it in around the dates already agreed.
Explain that translation was never part of the agreed scope, and that a separate piece of work would be needed.
Open his own piece list, work out what the request adds or repeats, and find which date it moves as a result.
Do the two best selling rooms in Tagalog as a goodwill gesture, and see whether the owner asks for the rest.

quiz.explanation: A chat thread cannot tell Joel what twenty pages of Tagalog costs him. His plan can. Twenty pages in a second language is new output, so opening the piece list to see what it adds and which date moves is what turns 'small tweak lang' into a fact the owner can actually decide on. Saying yes first and figuring out the fit later is exactly how a date slips without anyone choosing it to. Refusing outright skips a choice the owner is entitled to make. And doing two rooms for free quietly prices the other eighteen at nothing.

quiz.prompt: Marife agrees a change with a Davao client that adds two working days to their project, and writes it into that client's change log with the new delivery date. What still has to happen before the change is really absorbed?

options.text: The two days have to be laid onto the one list that spans every client, against the week they now sit in.
The original scope document should be reissued with the new deliverable and the revised date written into it.
The client should confirm the new delivery date in writing so the agreement is recorded on their side too.
The change log should record how long the extra work actually took, so that her future estimates improve.

quiz.explanation: Collisions never show up inside one client's board. Two days added in Davao land in a week that may already be sold to somebody else, and that is the failure that gets called disorganised two months later. Reissuing the whole scope is process for its own sake when a change note does the job. The client agreeing is already in the question. Logging the real duration is worth doing afterwards, but it protects the next project rather than this one.

quiz.prompt: Rowena is in week two of a bookkeeping catch up. Two months of bank statements she asked for have not arrived, and the agreed end date now depends on them. What should her message to the client contain?

options.text: A note that the statements are still outstanding, an apology for the slippage, and a promise to work weekends.
A short update saying the work is moving along, holding the bad news until she knows how late it will be.
A request for the statements today, with a warning that the end date will move if they do not arrive soon.
The missing item, the date it was due, the date now at risk, two real options, and when she needs an answer.

quiz.explanation: Count what each option actually gives the client to work with. A promise to work weekends buys a quiet week with Rowena's own time, and it is a promise she should not be making. Waiting until she knows exactly how late it will be spends the very week in which real options still exist. A warning with no options and no new date just reads as pressure, with nothing for the client to choose between. The one that works names the missing item, the date it was due, the date now at risk, two real options, and a date for the client's answer, all four parts an escalation actually needs.

quiz.prompt: In week one of a six week project, the first piece Kenneth finished took nearly three times as long as his record of timings said it would. Nothing else has been started yet. What should he do now?

options.text: Add an hour of buffer to each remaining piece, quietly, and hold on to the end date he already gave the client.
Re-estimate the pieces that are left against what that first one actually took, and see if the end date holds.
Carry on and see whether the next two pieces land closer to plan before he reacts to a single bad week.
Tell the client straight away that the project will be late and that a revised end date is being worked out.

quiz.explanation: One piece running long in week one is data about the whole estimate, not bad luck. Re-estimating costs an hour and tells you whether there is anything to raise at all. Waiting for two more data points spends the part of the project where options are cheap. Padding you cannot explain hides the problem from yourself as well as from the client. Announcing lateness before re-estimating raises alarm with nothing to decide, and the date may still hold.

quiz.prompt: A client Mila has worked with for a year asks her to add one line of copy to a product page. It really is ten minutes, nothing in the plan moves because of it, and she decides to do it. What else should she do?

options.text: Write it into that client's change log anyway, with the decided line reading absorbed and no date moved.
Send the change note first, with the options and the date it would move, and start once the client picks one.
Do it and say nothing, since logging a ten minute favour is more admin than the favour was ever work.
Do it and note in the next weekly update that it fell outside the agreed scope and was done at no charge.

quiz.explanation: Notice what the log entry actually buys Mila here. Absorbing a ten minute favour is often the right call, and writing it down, even as absorbed, no date moved, is what turns it from a leak into a recorded decision. The fifth time this same favour shows up, she is reading a list back instead of arguing from a feeling, and at renewal that list is the only proof any of it happened. Running the full change note process over ten minutes of work costs more than the task itself. Saying nothing leaves goodwill that nobody remembers later. Announcing it in the update turns a gift into an invoice, and still leaves nothing written down.

quiz.prompt: Danilo finishes an online store setup for a Pampanga seller. The store admin and the courier account were opened under his own email. The payment account is registered to the seller's own business documents and Danilo was added to it as a user. What does his handover have to do?

options.text: Move all three of the accounts into her name, and confirm in writing that every one of the transfers has gone through.
Send her the login details for each of the three accounts, so she can sign in to any of them when she needs to.
Move the two accounts he opened and stay on the payment account, since he is carrying on with monthly support work.
Move the store and courier accounts to her name, come off the payment account, and note what he no longer holds.

quiz.explanation: A handover is a transfer, not a delivery, and the client's business must not depend on your email address. But an account registered against her own documents cannot be signed over to her, because it is already hers, so the move there is Danilo coming off it. Transferring all three is not something he can do. Handing over logins to accounts still registered to him leaves him holding recovery access to her store. Staying on the payment account is a separate agreement, not a reason to keep a foot in her money.

quiz.prompt: Bea's client has just confirmed the work is finished and said it went really well. She wants more work out of this relationship. What is the strongest move right now?

options.text: Add the client to a mailing list and stay visible, so they think of her when something new comes up later.
Ask in one message for a testimonial about a specific part of the job, a referral, and the next piece of work.
Ask for the testimonial now, and leave the referral and any further work for a follow up in about a month.
Send the final invoice and let the work speak for itself, since asking for things this soon can look a bit pushy.

quiz.explanation: Timing is the whole answer here. The moment a client confirms the job is done is the highest their opinion of Bea will ever be, and it only goes down from there, so all three asks belong in that one message. Splitting them means the second ask lands weeks later in a colder room and reads as a follow-up sale. A mailing list is visibility, not a request. And letting the work speak for itself just means the client feels warmly and does nothing, because nobody actually asked them to.

quiz.prompt: Ramon asks a happy client for a referral at close out. The client replies "Sure, I'll keep you in mind," and nothing ever comes of it. What would have made that easier to act on?

options.text: Offering a discount to anyone the client sends his way, so there is something in the introduction for them too.
Sending a written summary of the work first, so the client had something concrete to forward to a business.
Naming the kind of business he wants next and asking whether anybody the client knows fits that description.
Following up two weeks later, since a busy client needs a reminder before an introduction actually happens.

quiz.explanation: Keep you in mind is what a vague ask earns. A specific one, naming the shape of business you want, turns the request into a question the client can search their memory for and answer yes or no to. A summary document gives them something to forward but still no idea who to forward it to. A discount makes the introduction feel transactional. Following up turns a favour you asked for into pressure, and costs you the goodwill you were relying on.

assignment.title: The operating pack for one client engagement
assignment.brief_mdx:
Pick one client engagement you could plausibly run and build the whole operating pack for it. Real is better than invented. A monthly social media retainer, a bookkeeping catch up, a website content build, an ecommerce store setup, an inbox and calendar retainer: any of these works, as long as the deliverables are things a person could actually hand over. Then submit the pack as text, in seven parts. Expect around a thousand words. Seven parts done properly do not fit in less, and a pack that fits in less has been written in generalities.

Everything below is about **your** engagement. A pack that would fit any client fits none, and a reviewer can tell in a minute.

1. **The engagement on one page.** Who the client is and what they asked for. Then the deliverables listed as things that can be handed over, the exclusions, what the client has to supply and by when, the assumptions you are planning against, and how many rounds of changes are included.
2. **What done looks like.** For each deliverable, the condition it has to be in before you call it finished, and the name of the one person allowed to say so. If the client's standard is currently a feeling, write the test you would replace it with.
3. **The plan.** Break the work into pieces, each with an output someone else could check and none running longer than about two working days. Put them in order, mark what blocks what, and mark the pieces blocked by the client rather than by you. Give every piece the date you work to. Give every deliverable the date the client is told, and show the cushion between them as its own line rather than hidden inside the pieces. Under the plan, in a few lines, say where your estimates came from. A job you have done before, a piece you timed, a stated guess: name it honestly for each.
4. **The status system.** Your states and the written definition of each, so that a task lands in the same state whoever sorts it. Where the work lives, and where the client's view of it lives. The fixed weekly reset: which day, and what you touch when you sit down to it.
5. **The week something slipped.** Write out one weekly update in full, for a week in which one date moved. Every line in it must trace back to an item on your board and its state, and the moved client-facing date is one of those lines. Then write the escalation message that goes with it, separately, as chapter 4 has it: what happened, what it affects, two real options, and what you need from the client by when.
6. **The change request.** Write the request the way a client would actually send it, in a chat message or an email. Then write your reply: what you understand is being asked, what it moves in time and in scope, and the choice you are putting to them. Finish with the one line you would add to your plan and the date that changes because of it.
7. **Handover and close-out.** The checklist you would run at the end, covering where the final deliverables live, which accesses and ownerships move out of your accounts and into theirs, which of them cannot be transferred at all so that you come off them instead, what needs a short walkthrough because the client has to operate it, and the loose ends you are naming rather than leaving. Then the close-out message: confirming the job is finished against your own definition of done from part 2, and the ask, made once.

Text only, no uploads and no design work. Change the client's name and any detail that identifies them.

One hard rule for the whole pack: no money figures and no invented facts. Write "the agreed fee" rather than an amount, and if a deadline comes from a government office, a platform or a payment provider, say the reader has to check the current one at the source rather than putting a number in. You are being marked on the arrangement, not on numbers you would have to make up.
criteria: Every deliverable carries a written condition for done and the name of one person allowed to say it is finished, and no deliverable is left with a feeling such as 'looks good' as its only test

Every piece in the plan has an output another person could check and a place in the sequence with its blockers marked, every piece carries a working date and every deliverable a client-facing date with the cushion between them shown as its own line, the source of each estimate is named honestly rather than left as a round number, and no fee, rate, percentage, platform charge or official deadline is invented anywhere in the pack

The exclusions, assumptions and client dependencies are specific to this engagement rather than generic, and each dependency carries an owner and a date so the schedule shows where it waits on the client

The status states are defined tightly enough that two people sorting the same task would land on the same state, the waiting state records whose turn it is and since when, and a fixed weekly reset day is named

The weekly update traces line by line to items and states on the board and states the moved date plainly rather than softening or holding it, and the separate escalation message carries what happened, what it affects, two real options and a dated ask

The change reply names what the request moves in time and in scope and offers a choice instead of a flat yes or no, and the handover moves access and ownership out of the learner's own accounts rather than only listing files
